title: Talking About People, Places, Conditions, and Comparisons

cover.alt: Two young friends sit on a green sofa with a ginger-and-white cat between them. One holds a blue ball for the cat. Two closed books lie on the table, and rain falls outside the window.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Welcome! This lesson has four parts. You will learn how to:
- use words like **him**, **her**, and **them** after verbs
- say what is in a place with **there is** and **there are**
- talk about conditions with **if**
- say that two things are the same with **as … as**
Each part has a short explanation with examples, then a test. Read the examples slowly and try saying them out loud.

items.prompt: Who do you often talk to after school? What do you talk about?
What things are in your room right now?
What will you do this weekend if the weather is nice?
Think of a friend or family member. Are you the same height as that person?

blocks.title: Part 1: Object Pronouns
paragraphs: A pronoun is a short word that takes the place of a noun. We use **subject pronouns** before the verb, and **object pronouns** after the verb.
| Subject (before the verb) | Object (after the verb) |
| I | me |
| you | you |
| he | him |
| she | her |
| it | it |
| we | us |
| they | them |
**Rule 1: Use an object pronoun after a verb.**
- I know **him**. (not *I know he.*)
- My mother loves **me**.
- These shoes are nice. I want **them**.
**Rule 2: Use an object pronoun after a preposition** (with, for, to, at, and others).
- I often play with **her**.
- This present is for **you**.
- Please listen to **us**.
**Tip:** First think about who the person is. One boy or man is **him**. One girl or woman is **her**. More than one person or thing is **them**. One thing is **it**.
- My uncle is funny. I like **him**.
- My aunt lives in a big city. I visit **her** every summer.
- I have a new bike. I ride **it** to school.

items.prompt: My sister is sad. I want to help ___.
items.explanation: Use the object pronoun her after the verb help to mean one girl or woman.

items.prompt: This gift is for my parents. I made it for ___.
items.explanation: Use the object pronoun them after the preposition for to mean more than one person.

items.instruction: Match each noun to the object pronoun.
items.explanation: Choose the object pronoun by thinking about who or what it is: one man is him, one woman is her, more than one is them or us, and one thing is it.

items.sourceJa: 彼女はよく私たちと遊びます。
items.explanation: After the preposition with, use the object pronoun us.

items.sourceJa: 私は彼をよく知っています。
items.explanation: After the verb know, use the object pronoun him.

items.sentence: My teacher is kind, so I like she.
items.explanation: Use the object pronoun her after the verb like.

items.prompt: I have a new phone. I use ___ every day.
items.hint: Use one object pronoun for one thing.
items.explanation: Use it after the verb use to replace one thing.

items.prompt: Please listen to me, Anna and Ken. Listen to ___.
items.hint: Use an object pronoun after to; it means you are speaking about yourself and others.
items.explanation: Use us after the preposition to for me and other people.

items.instruction: Replace the underlined-style noun phrase 'my cousins' with an object pronoun.
items.explanation: My cousins is more than one person, so use them after the verb visit.

blocks.title: Part 2: There Is and There Are
paragraphs: We use **there is** and **there are** to say that something is in a place.
**Rule 1: Use "there is" with one thing. Use "there are" with two or more things.**
- **There is** a cat on the sofa.
- **There are** two cats on the sofa.
- **There's** a clock on the wall. (There's = There is)
**Rule 2: Negative sentences use "there isn't" and "there aren't."** We often use **any** in negative sentences.
- **There isn't** a TV in my room.
- **There aren't** any eggs in the fridge.
**Rule 3: For questions, put "is" or "are" before "there."**
- **Is there** a station near here? — Yes, **there is**. / No, **there isn't**.
- **Are there** any books in your bag? — Yes, **there are**. / No, **there aren't**.
**Rule 4: To ask about a number, use "How many + plural noun + are there …?"**
- **How many** chairs **are there** in the room? — **There are** six chairs.
**Tip:** For short answers, use **there**, not **it** or **they**.
- Is there a bus stop on this street? — Yes, **there is**. (not *Yes, it is.*)

blocks.title: Grammar test: Part 2: There Is and There Are

items.prompt: ___ two cats on the sofa.
items.explanation: Use there are with two or more things.

items.instruction: Match each question with its correct short answer.
items.explanation: Short answers use there + is/are. For How many, answer with There are + number.

items.sourceJa: 私の部屋にはテレビがありません。
items.answer: There isn't a TV in my room
items.explanation: Use there isn't with one thing, followed by a.

items.sourceJa: あなたのかばんに本は入っていますか。
items.answer: Are there any books in your bag
items.explanation: For questions, put are before there. Use are with plural books.

items.sentence: There are a clock on the wall.
items.explanation: A clock is one thing, so use there is.

items.prompt: Is there a bus stop on this street? — Yes, ___ is.
items.hint: Write one word. Do not use it or they.
items.explanation: Short answers use there, not it.

items.prompt: There ___ any eggs in the fridge.
items.hint: Use a negative form for plural eggs.
items.explanation: Use there aren't with any and plural nouns.

items.instruction: Change the sentence to a negative sentence.
items.source: There are any eggs in the fridge.
accepted: There aren't any eggs in the fridge.
There are not any eggs in the fridge.
items.explanation: Make the negative with aren't and keep any.

blocks.title: Part 3: If Sentences
paragraphs: We use **if** to talk about a condition. A condition is something that may happen. The other part of the sentence tells the result.
- **If** it is sunny, we will go to the beach.
- Condition: it is sunny
- Result: we will go to the beach
**Rule 1: In the "if" part, use the present tense, even when you talk about the future.**
- **If** it **rains** tomorrow, I will stay home. (not *If it will rain tomorrow …*)
- **If** you **are** free, let's play a game.
- **If** she **gets** up early, she will catch the first train.
**Rule 2: The other part often uses "will," "can," or a request like "please" or "let's."**
- If you finish your homework, you **can** watch TV.
- If you have a question, **please** ask me.
**Rule 3: The "if" part can come first or second.** When it comes first, put a comma after it. When it comes second, you don't need a comma.
- **If** you are tired, you can sleep.
- You can sleep **if** you are tired.

items.prompt: If it ___ tomorrow, I will stay home.
items.explanation: In the if part, use the present tense even for the future.

items.prompt: If you have a question, ___ ask me.
items.explanation: The result part can be a request with please.

items.instruction: Match each condition with a natural result.
items.explanation: The if part gives the condition. The other part gives the result with will, can, let's or please.

items.instruction: Build the sentence. Start with If.
items.sourceJa: 明日雨が降ったら、私は家にいます。
items.answer: If it rains tomorrow, I will stay home.
items.explanation: Use the present tense (rains) after if, and put a comma after the if part.

items.sentence: If she get up early, she will catch the first train.
items.explanation: In the if part, she takes the present tense form gets.

items.prompt: You can sleep if you ___ tired.
items.explanation: Use the present tense are in the if part.

items.instruction: Put the if part second. Keep the meaning.
items.source: If you are tired, you can sleep.
accepted: You can sleep if you are tired.
items.explanation: When the if part comes second, you don't need a comma.

blocks.title: Part 4: As … As
paragraphs: We use **as + adjective + as** to say that two people or things are the **same** in some way.
**Rule 1: Use the basic form of the adjective between "as" and "as."** Don't use the "-er" or "-est" form.
- My bag is **as heavy as** your bag. (not *as heavier as*)
- This room is **as big as** that room.
- Today is **as cold as** yesterday.
**Rule 2: You can also use the basic form of an adverb.**
- My brother runs **as fast as** my father.
- I can sing **as well as** my sister.
**Rule 3: "Not as … as" means "less than."** It shows that two things are **not** the same.
- My dog is **not as big as** your dog. (Your dog is bigger.)
- This test is **not as difficult as** the last test. (The last test was more difficult.)
**Tip:** Always use **as** two times. Don't use **than** with as … as.
- She is **as tall as** her mother. (not *as tall than*)

items.prompt: My bag is as ___ as your bag.
items.explanation: Use the basic adjective between as and as.

items.prompt: This test is not as ___ as the last test.
items.explanation: Use the basic form, not a comparative or superlative.

items.instruction: Match each sentence start with the correct ending.
items.explanation: The pattern is as + adjective/adverb + as.

items.sourceJa: この部屋はあの部屋と同じくらい大きいです。
items.answer: This room is as big as that room
items.explanation: Use as + basic adjective + as.

items.sentence: She is as tall than her mother.
items.explanation: Use as ... as, not than.

items.prompt: I can sing as ___ as my sister.
items.hint: Use the adverb form of good.
items.explanation: The adverb of good is well: as well as.

items.prompt: Your dog is bigger, so my dog is not as ___ as your dog.
items.hint: Use the basic form of bigger.
items.explanation: Not as big as means your dog is bigger.

items.instruction: Change the sentence to the negative with not as ... as. Keep the meaning.
items.source: Your dog is bigger than my dog.
accepted: My dog is not as big as your dog.
My dog isn't as big as your dog.
items.explanation: Not as ... as means less than, so swap the subjects.

items.prompt: Talk about a friend or family member. What do you like to do with him or her?
Describe your town. What is there? What isn't there?
What will you do if you have a free day next week?
Compare two things you own, like two bags or two books. Are they the same in some way? Use as … as or not as … as.
